speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head P of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Home Team has developed a hard-earned reputation of maintaining a high standard of law and order in Singapore despite running a lean workforce.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are highly commendable outcomes that did not come easy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They arose through the blood, sweat and tears of our Home Team and MHA officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, circumstances are such that the Home Team cannot afford to sit on its laurels.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that it has, some time ago, in anticipation of a manpower crunch, expended efforts to set up the HTX and tap on technology, robotics and automation as force multipliers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The demands on Home Team, however, are ever rising.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How is the Home Team striking the right balance between the competing demands whilst it endeavours to keep Singapore safe and secure?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The ambition of security and safety appears to be simple, but it is anything but.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When the transformation in 2025 was announced in 2015, there were four planks which were discussed – manpower constraints, higher expectations of the public, increased load and emerging threats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The demographic decline of Singaporeans has meant that there were fewer each year to take up the role of Police Officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The ever-rising expectations of public; this is true, not just of policemen but of all public officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But, given the nature of the work that the police do – where the darkest, most secret part of human interactions come to light – the expectations of members of the public are escalated many folds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our officers must be a mix of psychologist, social worker, community partner, law enforcer and a friendly but authoritative face.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Added to all that – the policeman must be the hero next door.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because there is more work and more intense work, you cannot be an ordinary man or woman to be a Police Officer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The nature of crime the police now face, is not just the "traditional dangers" of crime such as violence or drug taking, but the new and rising threats such as cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, attacks are more difficult to pre-empt or prevent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are also exogenous and external challenges too, because Singapore is a porous country, and a global, transport, transshipment and financial hub.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What additional efforts will be taken to invest in and upgrade the skills of our Home Team officers?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How is it equipped to handle the ever more challenging cases for investigation, especially white-collar crime and scams?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Huge effort has to be expended in investigations before such perpetrators can be brought to book.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do recall that the hon Minister highlighting in this House the heavy workload of our Police Investigators and that he asked for review to get a better sense of the pressure faced by Police Officers, particularly due to lack of manpower resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How are we proposing to support our officers to ensure that not only their input will be of the highest quality in keeping with public expectation, but that their wellbeing is protected?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the Police has already started leveraging on technology and make significant progress.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They should have arms and legs of new pistols, new fighting skills, new sub-machine guns and carbines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Almost like Robocop, but perhaps a more friendly version of it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these require new skills and training, and people will be the key to the successful transformation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Police Officers already have hearts of steel – and we need to support, train and encourage these officers because they are few in number, even as the load becomes more heavy, the criminals more nefarious and public expectation ever higher.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, we need to ensure that there continues to be a high level of trust amongst Singaporeans on our Home Team's integrity and professionalism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, whatever transformation that will be undertaken will not work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I look forward to hearing the hon Minister's plans on supporting the Home Team Transformation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, the Singapore Police Force should be commended for its professionalism and hard won trust among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These can include the usage of robots, drones, biometrics and artificial intelligence to assist in investigations and also daily patrolling.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More such steps are needed to make our law enforcement system efficient and Singapore even safer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, my question is, what steps have been taken in that vein?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second cut, Sir, with COVID-19 disrupting many traditional methods of police work, there must have been strain on the effectiveness of certain ops.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Especially those that require physical contact and apprehension.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, the pandemic might have exposed key obstacles in relation to alternative methods of communication, resource management and crime, and service patterns.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Particularly, the safety and security of police officers and the communities they serve would be affected by the heightened risk of its exposure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has seen the closure of borders and limited travel between countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This situation has disrupted the usual movement of foreigners into and out of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as entry is concerned, new requirements for quarantine, purpose of entry and staggering the daily numbers allowed in have been imposed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for exit, limited modes of travel mean that short term visits may need to be extended repeatedly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even for those who have violated the law, or completed serving prison sentences, repatriation will be delayed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We see our residents facing such issues which require interfacing with the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) more intensively than before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For Singaporeans with foreign family members already in Singapore, repeated applications to ICA may have to be made for extension of visit passes due to lack of flights out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Others who want their family members to come in, face additional paperwork with the safe travel office.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of foreigners who are suspected to have broken the law or who have been convicted and sentenced, their continued presence in Singapore is not ideal and may pose additional risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For foreigners who are awaiting repatriation, have additional holding areas been needed to detain ex-prisoners who are awaiting return to their home countries?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, one of my Clementi residents came to me for help.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Middle-aged uncle, breadwinner, looking for a Security Officer Licence because he was retrenched from his previous job.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Agencies told him to submit the application online.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He was told he has to use SingPass, submit it through a website.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He was told to use a desktop PC to login, because the website operates a bit differently on a smartphone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But my Clementi resident is not IT literate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are residents looking for work, looking for a security licence, who do not have a smartphone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens to fellow Singaporeans like him, looking for a security officer job, but facing difficulty getting into the website?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another Clementi resident told me his story, also a breadwinner.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She’s a pillar of strength, caregiver, supporting at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So they cannot access ICA’s Electronic Permanent Residence website – the e-PR website.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When he appealed for help, the agencies told him, and I quote, “You can refer to the 'Step-by-Step Guide' on the e-PR system for more information on how to complete and submit your wife’s PR application online.” Sir, I believe the agencies meant well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But they did ask my resident to go online to access a guide on how to submit the application online.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He does not know how to go online.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, even as we move towards a smart nation and more technology, let us continue trying better to do better to improve.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When asked for a reason why they are not able to do so, among the responses are, they either do not have a computer, scanner and so on, and for those who have, they shared that they are not savvy enough to perform an online application.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Apart from not having computer facilities and online unfamiliarity, some mentioned language barrier as an issue, as the online application is only in English.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I do hope the Immigration and Checkpoint Authority (ICA) could provide better support in this area.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One suggestion is for ICA to work with People's Association in having a number of designated community centres, maybe one in each region, to provide the required facilities and other forms of support to Singaporeans who need such.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: LTVP+ provides access to additional benefits like subsidised healthcare and permission to work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, LTVP+ is not the same as Permanent Residency, or PR, in terms of benefits.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Of the many Singaporeans I meet at my Meet-the-People sessions, who are appealing for their foreign spouse's PR applications, the overwhelming majority of them are from the lower income groups, with spouses from countries like China, Vietnam and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are economic considerations and educational qualifications given more weight than family ties in determining PR application outcomes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, this would disadvantage the lower income.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their close kinship with Singaporeans makes them part of the Singapore Core.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And we as a society, should try to integrate them into our fold.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And are there plans to increasing the pool of interpreters, specifically those who speak Bahasa Indonesia, Tagalog, and Bengali, engaged by the police to ensure that as far as possible, when an accused person asks for a translator, one is available for the interview?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, in view of the recent Myanmarese Piang Ngaih Don's case, how is the police doing more to protect the vulnerable before the worst happens?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The case was a good reminder that religious extremism can come from anywhere, because any religion can be misused.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At a time like this, the population may need to be reassured that the Government is on top of things not only from an operational standpoint, but that Government policy is strictly secular and neither favours nor is influenced by religious beliefs from any quarter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Religious extremism when exposed, is obvious and rejected by all, including ordinary adherents of that religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is no danger that Government policy will be anything other than strongly against extremism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But is there a risk of the subtle influencing of policy by religious persons who are not necessarily radical?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, one issue the White Paper sought to deal with was insensitive proselytisation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Radicalism and extremism, not necessarily religion versus religion, but religion versus other communities, are subjects that deserve closer attention today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the principles stated in the 1989 White Paper and the worrying examples of that era, bear restating and updating because they are even more important now in our age of information silos.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper stated that paragraph 27, what I believe to be the critical point, and I quote, "The purpose of attempting to separate religion from politics is therefore not to determine the validity of various religious or ethical beliefs which have political or social implications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is to establish working rules by which many faiths can accept fundamental differences between them and co-exist peacefully in Singapore." Sir, far-right extremism has at its core, the rejection of the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Earlier this year, the owner of an eatery uploaded a video of a well-dressed man in office attire, throwing the rainbow LGBT pride flag at staff members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The flag was placed at the shop front.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The man allegedly told staff members, one of whom was hearing impaired, to I quote, "Go to hell", and accused them of being the kind of people who I quote again, "destroy Singapore".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Beyond this incident, it was concerning to read that one of the reasons the eatery owner uploaded the video was, and I quote, "to highlight the everyday reality that the LGBTQ community experience when most incidents are not even caught on camera." I am aware Minister for Home Affairs, in particular, has spoken up about the state's intolerance of acts perpetrated against the LGBTQ community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister has stressed that the Government's job is to protect everybody and warned race, religion or sexual orientation was irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Former Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong also made similar remarks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Chairman, across the world, we have seen attempts by hostile foreign actors trying to interfere with trying to interfere with other countries' domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have seen efforts to meddle with US elections, possibly even in the UK referendum leading to Brexit, and in many other aspects of domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Around the globe, many countries are stepping up their response to growing hybrid threats and disinformation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because of the great security threat, such interference can pose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What will MHA do to ensure that our domestic politics continues to remain free from such iniquitous influence?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Domestic politics and issues sensitive to Singaporeans should always be for Singaporeans alone to decide.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There have been reports that foreign interference can sway political and social outcomes in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore politics should always be the domain for Singaporeans alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Chairman, we live in an era where access to Internet is readily available anytime, anywhere.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Disinformation is easily sourced and used to influence others.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The risk of influence is higher upon youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This is compared to just more than a quarter across all age groups.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The online content he had accumulated, was sufficient for him to embark on an extensive plan, to target and harm Muslims.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: He was given various support, psychological and religious counselling by trained experts from the Religious Rehabilitation Group (RRG).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Misperceptions and misunderstandings of religion can thus lead to radicalisation among our youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: With increasing exposure among our youths to radicalised views and deliberate efforts of disinformation around the world, what are the steps and countermeasures taken by MHA to engage all our communities, better prepare our society and safeguard Singapore from such threats?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In light of recent high-profile detentions in Singapore, our ability to recognise and apprehend threats at an early stage is extremely crucial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With potential threats coming from self-radicalised individuals who can hide their motives even from friends and family, the nature of the fight against terrorism is evolving.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, with the advancement of technology and artificial intelligence, cyber terrorism is very real and multiplies the threat because potential threats are no longer local.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We must then operate within the international realm to combat alongside other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How are we improving our ability to detect threats both domestically and in the international theatre?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: ISD and the related agencies should be commended for their swift and prompt action in apprehending terror suspects and their effective tracking down of valuable leads.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The recent attention of a young 16-year-old boy who intended to attack two mosques is an example.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Having said that, after suspects are detained, the best course of action to take for the detainee and Singapore is to deploy resources to try to rehabilitate them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: While such detainees might have been radicalised through what they have watched and heard via the Internet, the process of rehabilitation can correct these views and allow them to become part of society again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What are the rehabilitation efforts that ISD and other related agencies have taken to bridge such a gap to detainees to help them reintegrate into society and reunite with their families?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Terrorism is a global threat with links throughout the world, with many terrorist networks and infrastructures stretching beyond a single continent and its ability to influence individuals and affiliated groups to stage attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our response must be a global one and in partnership with other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Notwithstanding the strains, COVID-19 has placed on operational capability, how are our agencies keeping up with ties, with like-minded agencies from other jurisdictions to fight the global threat of terrorism?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Fighting terrorism is not a singular effort, but one that requires a similar network to create the capability to make Singapore safer and less penetrable, especially in the age of cyber terrorism.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: At last year's Committee of Supply debate, my colleague, Mr Pritam Singh had proposed to consider the option of offering an automatic instalment plan for minor traffic offences, especially for those low-income who may not have the ability to pay up their fines in the single payment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Understandably, the intended effect of penalties is for offenders to be remorseful and regret their irresponsible acts and as a deterrence to ensure our roads are safe for all users.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Having said that, we should consider looking from the compassionate perspective, to minimise unintended effect of pushing this already struggling individual deeper into financial predicament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe we are aware of the circumstances where low-income Singaporeans had resorted to borrowing in order to pay for the traffic fines, when their appeal for instalment payment was unsuccessful.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I feel it does not lessen the intended effect of fines by allowing instalment payment for this group as eventually, they still have to bear the full amount.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: On the other hand, such compassionate consideration will be much appreciated as this will avoid further aggravation of their financial struggles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The recent Tanjong Pagar incident is a stark reminder of how a person who drives, is in charge of something very heavy and powerful, and one which, when dangerously or carelessly handled puts the driver's own life at risk, his fellow passengers at risk, pedestrians all around at risk, from those crossing the road or walking on the pavement or even waiting at the traffic light or sitting at a sidewalk cafe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Their actions leave a lasting impact on the victims' lives, their families and even sometimes, their own lives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, these pedestrians extend to the elderly and children.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have read reports and on social media of fatal accidents involving elderly and children including near misses; and these are one too many.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can MHA take a serious look at the various ways from a systemic approach and working closely with MOT and LTA including other Ministries such as MND and so on, on how we can further improve the current systems and prevent such mishaps from ever happening as they are not just happening at highways and major roads but also at various fringes of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I declare my interest as President of the Security Association Singapore, and director of a security company.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: There has been enthusiastic adoption of stage one technologies, that is technologies that assist security officers in carrying out their roles better.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Stage two and three technologies are focused more on reducing the reliance of the industry on manpower, and these have generally seen slower adoption.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: As we promote outcome-based contracting in the facilities management and security sectors, security agencies must adopt technology by either building their own in-house capabilities or, for smaller companies that find it difficult to build their own capabilities, to work with partners and to hunt in packs for contracts, comprising security consultants, manpower providers and technology companies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I am heartened that MHA and the Police Licensing Regulatory Department (PLRD) that regulates the security industry have taken a serious and consultative approach in converting the existing grading exercise for security agencies into a new competency assessment.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The previous grading exercise played an important role in kickstarting security agencies towards having better operational capabilities, proper manpower management processes and adopting technology.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The industry is far more responsible and mature now as compared to when the grading exercise first started.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: It will further hone the capabilities of an industry that performs functions and ancillary to the Home Team and a close partner of the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: This is a disturbingly high frequency and it is clearly an unacceptable situation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, the issue of drug abuse among our youths is an issue close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I have seen the severe damage and detrimental effects that young drug abusers can cause, not only to themselves but, more significantly, to their families and friends.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As a community, I believe that we have collectively supported the Government's tough stance against drug abuse over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The recent statistics for 2020 released by the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB), however, remains deeply worrying.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The statistics suggests a need to make even greater efforts to address the issue.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The worrying trend in the shift of mindsets towards growing narratives supporting liberal drug approaches further accentuates the problem.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, will developments such as the recent reclassification of cannabis and cannabis resin under the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs potentially change the attitudes of our Singaporean youths, towards the use of cannabis?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Careful consideration and firm steps must be taken to ensure that such mindsets do not take root in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I have also read the emergence of new psychoactive substances (NPS) which develops new chemicals that replace those that are banned, apparently in efforts to mimic the effects of established drugs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This development will surely add another complex layer to the rapidly evolving landscape of drug abuse, which the Home Team will need address.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I therefore invite the Minister to share with this House further details of the Ministry's plans on: (a) countering growing narratives supporting liberal drug approaches; (b) how to ensure that the NPS threat is kept under control; and (c) how to more effectively engage youths on the dangers of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: First, let me state that I completely agree with the hon Member, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I have seen this shift in culture of more tolerance towards drugs, especially in the last 15 years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I used to volunteer with SANA, the Singapore Anti-Narcotics Association, and there was not such a high degree of tolerance towards drugs 16 years ago as we are seeing here today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I want to first and foremost second what Mr Sitoh Yih Pin has just said.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We are seeing the shift in culture among youths to a more relaxed attitude towards recreational drug use.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With more youth acknowledging that legal consequences are a strong deterrent, we need to assist the CNB in the fight against the growing tolerance for recreational drug abuse and to raise awareness about the legal and health consequences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With new psychoactive substances constantly emerging, we must be proactive in recognising and banning such substances within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This assortment of drugs, such as synthetic cannabinoids, stimulants and opioids can be introduced to individuals willing to experience in order to discover possible new effects.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This means actually having to make very quick amendments to the Schedule in the Misuse of Drugs Act to catch out drugs that were not previously on the market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Next, Sir, Singapore has had a long battle against drugs and drug traffickers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have had to battle international criticism in continuing this policy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Yet, because of the heinous consequences to society and families, and our success – or relative success – in dealing effectively with the drug problem, our firm and relentless stance on traffickers must remain because we need to deter the international flow of drugs into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Continuing to keep Singapore drug-free is a growing challenge and to that end, we must continue to be vigilant in apprehending and anticipating drug traffickers and their movements even outside Singapore and, obviously, within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: My fourth and last cut, Sir, on drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Despite our hard stance against drugs, we want to rehabilitate and assimilate drug users back into our society and allow them reconnect and reunite with family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Seeing as there are many drug abusers who are youths and that number seems to be growing, from the statistics, how are we rehabilitating them and how successful has the rehabilitation initiatives such as peer support been?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, adult male offenders make up the majority of inmates and many have spouses and children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The point when an accused is incarcerated can be very destabilising on families and there are cases where both parents are incarcerated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My volunteers and I have met spouses so reliant on their husbands that they continue to seek instructions while they are in prison.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some divorcees despair as getting maintenance from the incarcerated exes can be difficult.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we appreciate the work done by the Yellow Ribbon Community Project, this is a touchpoint that is volunteer-driven and not a consistent or comprehensive solution – and some offenders opt out of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can measures be in place to support families better?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The first few months after release are critical for an ex-offender, during which the risk of becoming homeless and/or recidivism is high.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Hence, YRSG's strategy of securing employment and job retention is extremely crucial to re-integration efforts of ex-offenders into society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Beyond employment, a key part is also rehabilitation of ex-offenders with support of their families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Many studies have proven that family relationships play a pivotal role to prevent recidivism.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The situation is more pressing when dealing with ex-drug offenders who may face not only social stigma but other psychological issues.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: When I was volunteering with AMP Singapore, with the support of MHA, we launched the Development and Re-integration Programme, which provides individualised intervention plans and financial and socio-educational assistance for both the ex-offenders and their families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: It is important that services provided to the ex-offenders and their families are tailored to their individual needs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: With economic disruptions due to the pandemic and as strategic partners come under financial pressure to reduce their workforce, what are the steps taken by and future plans of MHA to rehabilitate ex-offenders, especially those with drug offences and to enhance their employability in this global pandemic and economic situation?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, I propose that MHA work with MOM to help recognise firms which practise inclusive hiring, including the hiring of ex-offenders.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A Yellow Ribbon Inclusive Hiring mark can be a way for fellow Singaporeans to recognise such firms and to show support.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: People can make the extra effort to support such firms, do business with such firms, contribute attention and profile to such firms.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: MHA can also work with MOF so that good inclusive HR practices are supported during the evaluation of Government tenders.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, if two bids are of equal quality, inclusive HR practices should be considered as a tie breaker.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Adding penal and Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) releases together, on the average, 9,862 inmates were released each year for this corresponding period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What is noteworthy is the overall recidivism rate has remained low and stable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: About eight out of 10 inmates released in 2018 did not return to prison within a two-year release period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is a good indication of the progress made in rehabilitating and re-integrating ex-inmates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: By no means, however, we should think we have arrived.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is not an easy target to achieve.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ex-inmates are debarred from certain sectors such as security and Government jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Lack of qualifications can be an inhibiting factor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Twenty-two percent of the convicted penal population only has primary school education or lower.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With the Government's decision to extend the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) to ex-offenders, I believe we have a unique opportunity to match ex-offenders to get and stay in better paying jobs with better prospects.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I note the tendency amongst some inmates to take on jobs in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I am concerned that they may, in due course, face difficulty with their housing and retirement needs if they do not accumulate sufficient savings in their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I also understand that Yellow Ribbon Singapore focusses more on long-term sentence ex-inmates and not short-term sentence ex-inmates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would be grateful if the Minister could please inform this House what is the average number of inmates referred to Yellow Ribbon Singapore per year between 2018 and 2020?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What is the breakdown between long-term and short-term sentence inmates?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As we gain more success in getting our inmates better paying jobs with better prospects, we also would have made significant progress in our efforts to help fellow Singaporeans in the lower economic strata to move up the social mobility escalator.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This group of vulnerable citizens could be exposed to bad actors online who may spread falsehoods about them, harass them or worse, damage their reputation online.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: These tortious harms affect people from young to old.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In simple language, many of us term this as cyberbullying or simply, cyber harassment.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: In specific cases like doxing, personal information is shared online to stir and facilitate harassment.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: What other measures would the Minister be planning to help those affected by such harmful speech online to achieve quick and effective justice?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Can MHA share plans and clarify if more expenditure has been factored for the Ministry to acquire more digitally equipped investigators and capabilities to ensure our law enforcement and connected agencies are sufficiently resourced and fit for purpose?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: My second point is about strengthening safeguards where at heart of the issue is about the need to approach this holistically, across the digital eco-system.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Given the many digital hand-offs, we need a multi-layered, whole-of-nation approach where all commercial participants in the digital economy supported by sharper laws and regulations are needed to protect our Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: As the Government and the Police cannot tackle this alone, what are the plans to work more with the relevant agencies and private sector participants apart from banks, such as telcos and e-commerce platforms to deal with this holistically?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Lastly, there is a need to address the trend in the movement of funds derived from scams to outside Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Chairman, I thank the hon Members for their comments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We continue to be one of the safest places in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People are confident that Home Team will carry out its mission fairly and effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleagues from my Ministry and I will try and deal with the points raised by the Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will first speak about our approach to religious harmony before setting out our transformation approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He raises the possibility of bias – now as well as in the future – and he asked, and I quote, "Is there a danger that laws and policies could be tilted towards particular religious beliefs by top civil servants?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If not now, maybe sometime in the future?" Mr Pritam Singh will accept, when his words are transmitted to the public, many will interpret him, in essence as saying that top civil servants could be biased and they could act in favour of religious communities because of their own religious beliefs, both now and in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would say leaving the public with that impression about our current top civil servants will be seriously wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are persons who have dedicated their entire lives to Public Service loyally and faithfully.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If there is evidence of such lack of integrity amongst current senior civil servants, then I agree, it should be raised and we must deal with it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the statement was meant only to cover a future possibility without any hint or suggestion of a lack of integrity amongst current top civil servants, then that should have been made crystal clear.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Since Mr Pritam Singh has raised an issue relating to the key foundations of Singapore and one of the key foundations of success, that is – the integrity of our senior civil servants.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The basic principle we follow and apply is that which Mr Lee Kuan Yew had set out in August 1965, and I quote, "We are going to have a multiracial nation in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Everyone will have his place, equal language, culture, religion".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Otherwise, in this small place, we will lose the trust of the people quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That goes for Cabinet Ministers, senior civil servants and the Public Service as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And when these principles are not observed, they must be dealt with.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is one of the key reasons Singapore is where it is now.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My Ministry, in particular, has a direct role in dealing with the issues relating to race and religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We formulate and implement policies which deal with these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have, over the years, worked with many senior civil servants – Permanent Secretaries and Directors of the Internal Security Department (ISD).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has given more than 35 years, his entire adult working life in the service of this country for the betterment of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It would be most unfair if he and his colleagues are tainted with the suspicion of religious bias without proof.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I emphasise, I am referring to the impressions that Mr Pritam Singh's words will leave with many and not what he may have actually meant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How the words could be understood, does matter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My current Permanent Secretary was Director ISD, Permanent Secretary of Law, then Permanent Secretary at MOT – 28 years in Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, an outstanding officer who is driven by only one aim, which is to make the lives of Singaporeans better.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We look for officers of this character and calibre and they should not in any way be tainted with suggestions of religious bias in their approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have highlighted officers from my Ministry in particular because we are at the forefront of dealing with religious issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We meet different religious leaders, we work hard to preserve religious harmony amongst their different faiths.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our integrity, honesty, reliability and neutrality are key to us and those are the currency we deal in.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Whether the people we work with accept us depends on these factors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And this is important in another central way: we promote officers on merit.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You do not want other questions to be asked – what is his religion?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Once we ask those questions for promotion, I think we will be in trouble.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not forget what I said in 2003 about leavening the effects of meritocracy by taking into account the position of minorities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What I say now can stand together with, and be qualified by, what I said in 2003.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Though the latter point, I emphasise, is a purely personal view.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or take another officer beyond the two I have mentioned: Esa Masood, He graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was formerly Deputy Director in MOE, Director at ECDA, now CE of MUIS.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For me, when a Police officer attends to a call at a house, you do not want people to think, "This is a Muslim officer" or "Christian officer" or "a Hindu officer".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You want people to think, "This is an Singapore Police Force officer".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I personally keep close track of trust levels in our Police Force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are now extremely high and we do not want to get to the levels of some First World countries where people march in the streets to abolish the Police Force because of racial issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not accidental that we have one of the highest levels of racial harmony in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The quality of our Civil Service, their integrity, is a key reason why Singapore has succeeded.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I also want to acknowledge, many of us have our own religious beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Not everyone is, or can be expected to be, a saint.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sometimes, there can be a tendency to see things through a religious lens or a personal perspective and that can apply to all – Ministers, civil servants, ground officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to avoid it, leave personal viewpoints and look at it when we are making public policy through a secular perspective, on what is the public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You will be informed by your religious beliefs, but you have to look at the broad majority and see what is in their interest.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to jealously guard against any such tendency to look through a particular lens, whether it is Ministers or anyone else and we have to set the tone from the very top.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Insist on the secular approach and be strict about that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh is reflecting, I think, what some people might feel but I will say to him today that it is not a systemic issue and we have to guard against it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It starts with politics, how we conduct it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And religion – how important do we make it in politics?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us be honest and ask how often have speeches done that in this House?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is the responsibility on both sides of the House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You want an example of where it can lead to?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the United States – how votes are sought along religious lines.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we go down that road, we will be in trouble.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked, "What of the future?" I will make two points.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One, we have, over the years, developed institutions, a system – the Public Service Commission (PSC), Public Service Divison (PSD), rules that seek to promote the best officers and weed out those whose integrity is not clear.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The assessments are multi-faceted and we have safeguarded the independence of the PSC, because the degradation of the Civil Service will seriously damage Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, having said that, my second point is, to be blunt whether the senior Civil Service remains world-class and has integrity depends ultimately on who the Ministers are too.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The timbre of our Ministers will ultimately decide everything else.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Ministers are biased, they lack integrity, then that will spread, maybe slowly but surely.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The institutions that we have set up can delay the spread.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It may depend on how long the top remains bad, but it would not be a happy situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have avoided these outcomes so far and you only have to look at some countries outside of Singapore, many countries, including First World countries to see what can go wrong and how quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, Mr Singh spoke about our LGBTQ community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was emphasised by me during the MRHA's Second Reading, and also during my speech at last year's Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Regardless of which community, what your social, religious or sexual beliefs are, everyone will be protected here, and I have said so categorically.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are not any lesser by reason of our sexual preferences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if anyone stirs hate speech either for or against any sexual or religious community, we will take action; does not mean action will be taken on every occasion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police will use their discretion and assess the context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If Mr Singh thinks that there should be any change or variation to this position, I will be happy to hear from him.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In particular, if he wishes to clarify what exactly is his position on our LGBTQ policies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will be happy to hear from him.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third point that Mr Singh made, was on secularism and he asked for a statement.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our secular stand has been made clear when the Government looks at policies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last year, in November, at the Religious Rehabilitation Group seminar, I set out how our secular approach works.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I also explained how our approach, for example, differs from the French approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have spoken about our approach at least nine times over the last five years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I do not think Mr Pritam Singh wants a tenth speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I can give Mr Pritam Singh the references.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fourth point he makes is updating the MRHA White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I can assure Mr Singh – religious issues, interaction of religious communities, is a top of mind issue for us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In April 2019, I delivered a very substantive Ministerial Statement, titled "Restricting Hate Speech to Maintain Racial and Religious Harmony in Singapore".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I explained the Government's position and approach in dealing with hate and offensive speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then, we went further than a White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In June 2019, the same year, with the support of the Government, our religious leaders worked together on a "Commitment to Safeguard Religious Harmony".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They affirmed the shared values and the way of life of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This approach has underpinned the religious harmony we have.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would invite a careful study of this very important document.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a commitment by the major religious groups and organisations on the principles of religious harmony that should govern us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It goes beyond past declarations of religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It details the many positive ways in which Singaporeans have been interacting across religions and it encourages Singaporeans of all faiths to practise tolerance and acceptance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, allowing each other to profess our faiths and to do so in a respectful manner; eating together with others, even if we have different religious dietary requirements and practices; and attending the life events of others, such as weddings and funerals, even if those are held in the place of worship of that faith.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it can be seen: we have reviewed the 1989 White Paper we have taken concrete steps after that Review.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have considered the evolving context, brought religious groups and leaders together, affirmed a new document of principles and have amended the MRHA.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, if you are a non-religious leader and you said something in a private context, that may not be an offence, but if the same thing were to be said by a religious leader, the defence is much narrower.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has got to show that it was only a domestic communication between the leader and his relatives or member of his household.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it is an issue which we will keep reviewing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They allow us to examine again some key and important points.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pillai asked, how will the Home Team balance increasing demands on it given the manpower issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have said before – there is a limit to increasing our resources and manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is in short supply all across Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Chairman, with your permission, may I display a set of slides on the LCD screen as I make my points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: HTX has 14 centres of expertise in a number of areas: biometric, sense-making and robotics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is also developing expertise in managing data centres and cloud-based technologies and a Security Operations Centre, with 24/7 monitoring will be set up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are enhancing our frontline response through greater use of cameras.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has been a game-changer to deter, investigate and solve crimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Surveys have shown that people feel safer with a prominent placement of police cameras in their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the next several years, I promise that many more cameras will be installed across the island subject to the budgetary situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, Police have redesigned our Neighbourhood Police Centres and Police Post to include automated self-help kiosks, so people can access police services around the clock.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will have cameras which will provide a 360-degree view of its surroundings to the Police Command Centre, and it will allow commanders at the Command Centre to assess the situation and deploy back-ups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The cars will also have video analytics tech to read number plates and automatically flag vehicles of interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we will be surrounded by sensors which make people feel safer and more confident.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, Police have deployed two Police Beacon prototypes at Sengkang and Punggol for a year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police Beacons will allow members of the public to contact the Police directly during emergencies and they will come equipped with a range of tools to create deterrence and project presence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the situation can be assessed immediately, quickly, and they are particularly useful in more secluded locations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond sensors, in terms of investigations, Police and CNB are working to sharpen the investigation capabilities with tech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, their investigation and case management systems are being digitised, automated and streamlined, so that officers can access information and update cases on the move instead of having to go back to the office to do it, and save time on handling paperwork and admin tasks because the tool will be an integrated search tool, searching multiple databases at one go.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, Mr Pillai asked how are the Police adapting to tackling some of the most challenging cases of scams and commercial crimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police are seeking to use tech again, for example, automated screening of financial transactions when investigating scams.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They also have tools to quickly extract and analyse digital evidence from mobile devices, thumb drives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think Members will understand – in the end there is a limit to how much can be done when the scammers are overseas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three, I will deal with the tech and our emergency responses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SCDF, for example, is building the next generation Smart Fire Stations, starting with the new Punggol Fire Station.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will make greater use of sensors and automation to help with manpower management, operational response and decision-making.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Manual processes, like tracking the readiness of emergency supplies vehicles, rostering of duty personnel, will all be automated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During an emergency, an Artificial Intelligence system will send critical information – floor plans of buildings, live video feed of the site to our officers, where available – even before they arrive at the site.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will help officers assess the situation, develop a plan faster and enhance their response.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our SCDF officers will also be having smart wearables that will be integrated with the Smart Fire Station's systems, and it will allow commanders to monitor officers' physical condition during operations and training to reduce risk of injury.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, our paramedics will be able to access patient data from MOH databases when responding to a 995 call.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will allow for more effective medical intervention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our aim is to have travellers move through automated lanes when they enter and leave Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the necessary tech has already been put in place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is more secure than fingerprint clearance and also contactless.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The traditional paper-based card system has been replaced by the SG Arrival Card e-service and mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That facilitates smoother immigration clearance and enhances the advanced screening of passenger info.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regard to the iris and facial images we intend to upgrade this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will verify travellers' identities through iris and facial images at the automated lanes instead of passports and thumbprints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked how is ICA managing new demands arising from COVID-19 and how foreigners are held following their release from prison if they cannot be repatriated immediately, and whether additional manpower was required.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ICA has been putting in place plans and systems to cope with the new demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It enabled them to cope with the new demands brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The digital services can adapt to changes to our border control rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are designed to enable ICA to administer relevant measures for different groups of travellers and also enables integration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, ICA integrated Electronic Health Declaration Cards into the SG Arrival Card platform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regard to the question on repatriation of foreigners, ICA will seek to repatriate them as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, of course, this is subject to the availability of flights and COVID-19 border control measures both here and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where necessary, ICA will house them temporarily in existing prisons or other ICA facilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some additional manpower was needed to resource new functions, but ICA has largely coped by redeploying officers to meet the new demands, like the Safe Travel Office and enforcing the Stay-Home Notice regime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the surge of travellers comes back, there is obviously going to be substantial demand on ICA and we will have to deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim has asked about morale of ICA officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ICA has implemented additional measures to support the ground officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senior commanders engage officers regularly, to gather feedback and try to address their concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, not every single concern can be addressed but the serious engagement and attempt to solve the issues properly are important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The vision is to have a smart prison that leverages technology to automate routine work, so that prison officers can be more focused on inmates' rehab.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For that, one, they go to smart cameras and video analytics, which will assist officers in monitoring inmates' activities, movements, detect irregular behaviour such as fights and medical emergencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, technology is also helping substantially with rehabilitation of inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are given mobile tablets, with e-books and guiding resources to supplement their regular lessons and programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It allows the inmates to learn at their own pace and take greater ownership of their rehab.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are developing a mobile app for supervisees in the community, to reinforce their learning and rehab.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The supervisees can use the app to access customised e-resources, keep track of their progress and look for job opportunities and community support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want to allow more inmates to serve a larger part of their sentences in the community, as long as it is safe to do so, so that they are out for longer period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that can be done, we think, through greater use of technology to monitor the inmates in the community and help compliance with supervision conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is more discreet than the ankle tag that many Members might be aware of.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It reduces the stigma, it boosts the supervisee's self-confidence and helps re-integration back into society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisons has also enhanced its digital case management system, making it easier for community partners to access case files and share updates with Prisons staff.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr de Souza asked how the Police seek to overcome operational constraints posed by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Drones and robots were deployed for security operations at COVID-19 isolation facilities, which reduced the risk of exposure for our frontline officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SCDF has been using robots to fight fire.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At an industrial fire in Tuas in March last year, these robots tackled the most dangerous parts of the fire, with immense heat and poor visibility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Home Team will continue to build on these capabilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police have, likewise, deployed drones and robots at major public events for crowd management and public safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will also support officers in their daily patrols.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In future, you may see three SCDF officers and a robot responding to a fire on board the "Red Rhino", instead of the current four-man section.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These robots are capable of pushing deeper into the seat of the fire, and can help to carry equipment and casualties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are also enhancing our ability to deal with the threat of drones.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police are also exploring how to equip the next-generation FRCs with counter-drone capabilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ICA, for example, is bringing more of its services online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, residents can register or re-register for their Identification Card online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can also update their address online, instead of visiting the ICA Building or a Police Post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ICA will also introduce push notifications for all Singapore residents with registered SingPass accounts, to remind them to follow up on transactions with ICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, you may receive a reminder to re-register your Identity Card on your 30th or 55th birthday.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Faisal Manap spoke about not excluding those who lack IT access or are less IT-savvy from Home Team services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We try to design our e-services to be simple, seamless and convenient for everyone and we will also try and assist those who need help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they need physical channels, we will provide helpdesks, self-help kiosks, and service centres.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Specifically, Dr Tan raised about Security Officer Licence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who want assistance can call the Police Licensing and Regulatory Department to make an appointment, or visit their service counter during office hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For Citizenship and PR applications, those without Internet access can visit the Citizen Connect Centres (CCCs) for free access to Internet-enabled computing devices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who require more assistance can approach ICA officers at the ICA Building.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members of the public will be served at a single counter for all services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will also try and make it a more seamless customer experience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about our plans to upgrade the skills of our officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Home Team Academy has been using the Home Team Simulation System to train our officers in managing large-scale security incidents and joint operations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires fewer resources to carry out than a physical training exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The approach is always to try and upgrade the skills and make the training more realistic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are also other new developments that continue to drive up demand for the Home Team’s manpower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, while ICA uses technology, it still needs manpower to run operations at future checkpoints – Tuas Mega Port and the RTS Link.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SCDF, too, will need more ambulances and more officers to attend to the growing number of medical emergencies, due to our ageing population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police will need to expand the deployment of In-Situ Reaction Teams (IRTs) to patrol high footfall locations in Singapore to swiftly respond to armed terrorist attacks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also need to increase the number of Police investigators.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of investigation files handled by Land Divisions increased by 36% between 2015 and 2019.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perpetrators, often anonymous, may often be based overseas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires much more effort to track and identify them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked how we are supporting the well-being of our Investigation Officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Apart from increasing the number of investigators to manage the workload, Police are currently undertaking an internal review of their systems, processes and structures to see how better we can support our investigators.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will see from what I have said that Police, the Home Team as a whole, have been exploring and investing in technology for some time, even before COVID-19, and that has stood us in good stead during COVID-19 and we will continue on that path.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Police have kept traditional crimes, that is, all crimes except scams, well in check and on the decline over the years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The drug situation in Singapore remains under control, and our fire fatality rate remains one of the lowest in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Public confidence in the Home Team remains high.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Notwithstanding these successes, there are a few key challenges we are paying particular attention to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are terrorism, foreign interference and harmful online content.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team has been vigilant, but the terrorists only need to get through once to cause us serious damage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Christopher De Souza asked about our detection abilities and rehabilitation of terrorist detainees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have strong working relationships with foreign security agencies to share intelligence and disrupt plots.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Local threats are more difficult to detect as individuals may be self-radicalised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under the SGSecure movement, the Home Team and our partners make efforts to educate the community on preventing and responding to terror attacks, including spotting the signs of radicalisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On terrorist detainees, the best way to neutralise their threat is to rehabilitate and reintegrate them into society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have refined our approach based on our own experiences, learning from international best practices and in response to the changing profile of detainees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked what MHA would do to deter foreign interference in our domestic affairs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He believes we should ensure that Singapore politics remain the domain of Singaporeans only.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have previously articulated the need to safeguard Singapore against foreign interference in our domestic politics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But in recent times, it has risen in potential and severity because of the increasing ease to carry out such operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since time immemorial, states have sought to subvert others to achieve their own objectives and agenda.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This can take various forms, such as hostile information campaigns and subversion operations to manipulate domestic political discourse, and to influence politically significant organisations and persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is also value to polarising views and turning people against each other.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Doing so can weaken a country’s resolve and strengthen the attacker’s bargaining position.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore needs to be open to the world to make a living.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But our diversity and openness also present opportunities for foreign actors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the 1970s, we were the target of two interference operations involving our newspapers – The Eastern Sun and the Singapore Herald.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The newspapers received funding from foreign sources and ran articles to undermine our nation-building efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2018 and 2019, when we were facing bilateral issues with our immediate neighbour, there was a curious spike in online comments critical of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many of these comments came from anonymous accounts, which sought to give an artificial impression that there were significant and fundamental objections to Singapore's position.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In recent years, we have seen concerning developments overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, if you compare the two time periods, a six-fold increase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also seen reports from Australia and other countries that foreign powers and their agents attempted to influence their politics by buying off political parties and politicians.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, social media platforms have not dealt, and have little interest to deal with these threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For instance, political observers have attributed the storming of the US Capitol to the failure of social media platforms to take timely and firm action against election misinformation and calls for violent resistance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fortunately for us, 2020’s Parliamentary Elections went peacefully.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, looking at other countries, there is reason for more robust preventive measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many countries have taken steps to mitigate this risk.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some have introduced legislation to address the threat of foreign interference.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For instance, Australia has made it compulsory for those who undertake activities on behalf of foreign principals to make public disclosures to deter covert attempts to influence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
