text: To address the threat of foreign interference in our domestic politics, we must, in the first place, build up Singaporeans’ ability to discern legitimate and artificial online discourse, and respond appropriately.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as interference operations are increasingly sophisticated and well-disguised, it is not enough to have a discerning public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, to obtain necessary information to investigate hostile information campaigns to determine if they are of foreign provenance or artificial; to break the virality of such campaigns if they are, indeed, conducted by foreign actors to subvert our domestic politics; and to carry counter-messaging to alert Singaporeans to these on-going hostile information campaigns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, what levels of transparency in funding, support and leadership are appropriate?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The public has a big part in this to shape proposals and to give the eventual safeguards their strongest support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is the only way we can effectively deter bad foreign actors from exploiting our vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked about achieving effective justice for those affected by online harassment and doxing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about the steps to protect our society from harmful online content.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another example would be the dissemination of voyeuristic material and intimate images without consent through platforms, such as Telegram.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some platforms do put in effort to deal with harmful content.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But not every platform puts society's interests first.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is to be expected – platforms are driven by their own values and commercial interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many countries, therefore, see the need for regulation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many tech companies acknowledged the need for regulation even if they disagree with governments on the "how".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA has been working with MCI to review our options.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To effectively carry out the many streams of work, public trust in the Home Team is critical.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do not take this trust for granted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Home Team will continue to uphold the highest level of integrity and conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where there are allegations of improper discharge of duties by Home Team officers, we will investigate thoroughly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If the allegations are substantiated, firm action is taken against the officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where we have slipped up as an organisation, we have acknowledged unreservedly and tightened up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sadly, there have been efforts by some people to de-legitimise our Police and other law enforcement agencies by circulating false allegations through social media.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These irresponsible social media posts seek to weaken public trust in the Home Team and weaken our ability to maintain law and order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need the public's help to be responsible and refrain from spreading false allegations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to improve our processes to better serve the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where it was initially only used for investigation of rape offences, it now covers other offences, such as child abuse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: VRI requires substantial investment in technology, infrastructure and, most important of all, training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will gradually expand the types of offences to be covered by VRI.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are budgetary constraints as we move on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If a person requires interpretation, the Police will engage an interpreter and record the statement only when the interpreter is available.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our safety and security landscape is getting more challenging.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been doing quite well and will invest more resources to tackle emerging threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to do what it takes to uphold the trust of Singaporeans through our capabilities, integrity and impartiality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will need the strong support of fellow Singaporeans and must be able to count on this.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister of State Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Some Members today are wearing the anti-drug collar pin here and the Yellow Ribbon collar pin to demonstrate their support of our national efforts in these areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The global drug situation continues to be worrying.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This may lead some to believe that cannabis is harmless, despite strong evidence to the contrary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: More needs to be done to safeguard our zero-tolerance policy towards drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Preventive drug education is our first line of defence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Central Narcotics Bureau, or CNB, educates Primary and Secondary school students about the dangers of drugs through activities like talks and competitions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB continues to partner students from Institutes of Higher Learning to co-create projects to encourage older youths to become anti-drug advocates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For instance, CNB worked with Ngee Ann Polytechnic students on a social media marketing campaign, YouUseYouLose, which reached almost 300,000 people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, information on the harms of cannabis was pushed out as advertisements, and a short film on cannabis was produced and screened in cinemas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue our efforts to counter narratives that downplay the harms of drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza spoke about halting the international flow of drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: CNB works with regional counterparts to share intelligence and conducts joint operations to deal with transnational drug activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Home Team has strong enforcement measures at our borders to detect traffickers and drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin mentioned new psychoactive substances, or NPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about rehabilitating youth drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Youths are placed on the Youth Enhanced Supervision Scheme or channelled to the Community Rehabilitation Centre or Drug Rehabilitation Centre (DRC), depending on various factors, such as their assessed risk level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Each youth is matched to the most appropriate intervention programme to best support their rehabiliation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked about the rehabilitation and re-integration of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2014, the Enhanced Drug Rehabilitation Regime, or EDRR, was introduced for first- and second-time drug abusers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This aligned rehabilitative interventions to the abusers' risk of re-offending and level of dependency on drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2019, the drug rehabilitation regime was further enhanced to commit third-time and subsequent drug abusers who are not charged with any other criminal offences to the DRC, instead of being charged in Court and made liable for long-term imprisonment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for the effectiveness of this calibrated approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will assess the effectiveness of the 2019 enhancements when we have sufficient data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Effective rehabilitation and re-integration requires strong community, family and vocational support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will speak in Malay about community support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):    The Malay/Muslim community has made progress in the fight against drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The relapse rate of Malay drug abusers within two years after release has decreased from 42% for the 2011 release cohort, to about 30% for the 2018 release cohort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue our work to bring the numbers down even further.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under the “Dadah Itu Haram” campaign, the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) collaborated with mosques and community partners to conduct outreach activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MUIS set up the Family and Inmates Through-care Assistance Haven office, or FITRAH, to provide comprehensive support for inmates and their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Currently, volunteers from FITRAH undergo training to equip them with a broad range of skills, such as counselling, so that they can support their beneficiaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will consider Ms Nadia’s suggestion to prepare FITRAH volunteers so that they can befriend inmates of different backgrounds and needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under Prisons’ Throughcare Volunteer Framework, volunteers who have built rapport with the inmates through regular incare programmes can continue to provide pro-social support for them after their release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There are groups of ex-offenders who have banded together to support one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This year, the CARE Network will establish a framework to support such groups, which can serve as pro-social networks for ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to work closely with community groups to strengthen our outreach and reintegration efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In English) Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin asked what more can be done to support families of inmates and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For families of inmates who need support, Prisons will make referrals to Family Service Centres (FSCs) or other social service agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This year, Prisons and MSF will strengthen coordination and information exchange with FSCs on inmates with family members in need of support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will ensure timely access to FSC resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Besides training volunteers who work with inmates, Prisons will extend training opportunities to those who assist inmates' families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Together, our efforts to better support families will also help to reduce inter-generational offending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked about enhancing the employability of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: YRSG has also mapped a skills masterplan, under which it has developed pathways for inmates to continue to acquire skills after release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2020, YRSG partnered organisations to offer training in media and precision engineering.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This year, TAP and Grow will be expanded to the logistics and infocomm sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Training facilities for these sectors will be set up in prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This has expanded the employment opportunities available to ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about encouraging short sentence inmates to take advantage of the increased job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: YRSG offers career guidance and job matching to all inmates, regardless of the length of their sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Of these, about 5.5% served short sentences, with the rest comprising long-term or DRC inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: YRSG and Prisons will intensify outreach to create greater awareness of the opportunities available and we will take Mr Murali Pillai's suggestion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng suggested introducing a Yellow Ribbon mark to recognise firms that practise inclusive hiring of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have been recognising such employers through the previous SCORE Appreciation Awards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Nonetheless, a Yellow Ribbon mark could encourage more employers to partner with YRSG and offer more employment opportunities to ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: And I thank Dr Tan Wu Meng for his suggestion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: On immigration, Mr Gerald Giam asked about permanent residence for foreigners with family ties to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Each PR application is evaluated holistically on a range of criteria, including but not limited to economic contributions, educational qualifications and applicant's ability to integrate into society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In general, PR applicants with family ties to Singaporeans are already considered more favourably to those without.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Foreigners with family ties to Singaporeans who are not able to obtain PR but wish to continue residing in Singapore may apply for a Long-Term Visit Pass, work pass or Student Pass.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Parliamentary colleagues, thank you for your strong support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With your continued support and that of all Singaporeans, the Home Team will continue to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This coming year, MHA will tap on our partnership with the community in two areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, in the design of our policies and legislation related to the private security industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are concerned with the scam situation in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We agree with Mr Derrick Goh that the Police should be sufficiently resourced to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Police have since re-organised existing resources and set up the Anti-Scam Centre (ASC) in 2019.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through the Transnational Commercial Crime Task Force, or TCTF, the Police have also partnered foreign law enforcement agencies in Malaysia, Macau and Hong Kong to tackle cross-border scam syndicates targeting victims in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Police will continue to conduct joint operations with like-minded jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And MHA will continue to monitor and review the resources allocation to ensure that the Police continue to remain effective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I chair the Inter-Ministry Committee on Scams, or IMCS in short, which draws on the expertise and the resources from different Ministries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the coming year, the IMCS will deepen our partnership with the community and private sector stakeholders to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Allow me to elaborate on a few notable initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked for an update on the IMCS' plans to deepen its partnership with the banks, telcos and digital platforms to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Association of Banks in Singapore, or ABS, and its members have worked with the Police and MAS to detect and to weed out scammers and money mules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We also took measures to help victims recover losses through Project FRONTIER, which stands for Funds Recovery Operations and Networks Team, Inspiring Effective Resolutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is a collaboration between Police and more than 20 financial institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I have asked banks if we can work together to further compress the turnaround time for freezing of bank accounts used by scammers so that even less is lost to scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Besides banks, we also work closely with telcos and IMDA to block spoof calls and scam websites used by overseas scammers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: MCI will elaborate on efforts to tackle scam calls during its Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are working with e-commerce platforms, such as Carousell, Lazada, Shopee, Qoo10 and Amazon to prevent scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Areas being explored are improving the seller verification and increasing the use of more secured payment methods, such as escrow accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A few overseas jurisdictions have begun exploring the use of legislative levers to place clear obligations on the industry to secure e-commerce transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, in December 2020, the EU Commission proposed the Digital Services Act to better regulate the digital space, including online platforms and intermediaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Government is considering all options to address the scourge of e-commerce scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While efforts to disrupt scammers' operations and money transfers are key to combating scams, the best defence against scams is a discerning and vigilant public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Everyone can potentially be a victim, not just the elderly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is important for everyone to exercise vigilance, to be sceptical of incredulous promises and unverifiable requests and check with authorities whenever in doubt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I also encourage everyone to download ScamShield to filter out scam calls and messages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: ScamShield is an application developed by GovTech, MHA as well as NCPC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But right now, it is only available in iOS version but agencies are working towards developing an Android version.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):    Mdm Chairperson, the number of scams in Singapore is on the rise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Thus, the Home Team will step up efforts to work closely with our community partners to strengthen the public’s awareness of scams and scam prevention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There are three “Don’t”s in scam prevention: first, don’t trust strangers; second, don’t reveal your passwords; third, don’t transfer funds carelessly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Lately, loan scams have been on the rise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, according to our laws, a licensed moneylender cannot approve or grant a loan to a borrower remotely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In other words, those who claim to be licensed moneylenders offering loans to you via the phone or through Whatsapp messages must be scammers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: When faced with a situation that raises suspicion, members of public can view the list of legitimate financial institutes published on the Registry of Moneylenders’ website.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Members of public can also visit the App Store to download Scamshield to screen and block calls and messages suspected to be from scammers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In English): I will now talk about engaging community on policies and legislation related to the private security industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked how the new Security Agencies Competency Evaluation or SACE framework will encourage transformation and adoption of technology by the private security industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A key assessment area under the SACE will be on how much security agencies harness technology to augment critical areas, such as training, operations, and command, control and communications (C3).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This will set new benchmarks for the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These competencies will be reviewed periodically to keep up with technological developments and complement efforts under the Security Industry Transformation Map (SITM).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In addition, we will continue supporting public education efforts, such as the industry-led anti-abuse campaign.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: MHA will also work with the industry to equip security officers with better public management skills and encourage the use of body-worn cameras to further deter abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I will also address two questions on road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Faisal Manap asked whether drivers in financial difficulty can be allowed to pay their road traffic fines in instalments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: MHA has been studying this since last year as we have also received feedback from several Members of this House.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Regardless, already today, for genuine cases of financial difficulty, if the individual appeals to Traffic Police (TP) and the appeal is assessed to be meritorious, TP will extend their deadline to pay the traffic fine.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Patrick Tay spoke about the need for greater traffic safeguards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That said, we agree with Mr Patrick Tay that every accident is one too many.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will continue to do more to enhance road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are completing our review and will announce details later in the year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have three points to make in response to Minister's speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first pertains to the point that my cut could have been interpreted to mean that some civil servants are biased.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it is important that I make it clear that I am not suggesting that they are, nor do I mean to undermine their work and their morale.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My motivation was to really seek a restatement of the Government's commitment towards secularism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I thank the Minister for dealing with the speech and the Government's approach to what I said in a very detailed way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I did not realise the Minister had made these remarks nine times since 2015.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Suffice to say, I appreciate his tenth restatement more than anything.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The third point I wish to make concerns the Minister's latter comments about up to 90,000 more cameras coming on stream, provided the Budget allows for it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it will be foolhardy to try and stop and prevent the usefulness of technology in the support of the work of the Home Team to resolve crimes and matters of that regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, in that sense, I can support it because it will help the Police's work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I would caution, as I have done before in other speeches, is to restate how the algorithms behind some of these cameras are managed and guarded, because if that information leaks, if it goes out, I think it can damage public confidence in some of this technology that the Home Team seeks to introduce.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first two points, I am glad that Mr Singh and we see eye-to-eye and he agrees with us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason is this – and I take entirely the point about making sure that the information that is obtained, is used properly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, ICA has a lot of information – identity card, registration, travel – and we need to make sure that that information is used properly and not given to unauthorised persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think this issue of privacy, sometimes the way one has got to analyse is – if individual A says something to individual B in his home, that is private.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is no one's business to know what you have said to your wife to, or to your son, or to your friend at your home.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If supposing the Police are investigating a crime, they are entitled to come to your house and ask what you have said, if it is relevant for the investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you are duty-bound to say it and you cannot say "my right of privacy".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And whoever you spoke with also will have to disclose, subject to, you know, arguments about privilege against self-incrimination and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you did something in a public place, the Police are entitled to go in and investigate you and ask you what you did.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is reason to believe a crime was committed, they are entitled to investigate and ask everybody else what they saw and then bring that evidence to Court, if necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The cameras, to some extent, either short circuits or supplements that approach, and that is the way to approach these sensors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why the vast majority of our public actually welcome these cameras.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The first is in regard to radicalised youths.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I think this question would be for Second Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Perhaps, can we get some clarity as to what would be MHA's rehabilitation approach for radicalised youths?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: My second clarification is in respect of the rehabilitation and reintegration of ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: If I may ask Minister of State Faishal Ibrahim, he covered it in his speech.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: How has COVID-19 affected the number of ex-offenders and inmates securing jobs right before release or after release?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope it is okay for me to just take a step back and explain our approach to rehabilitation in general and then to focus on the approach for youths.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our goal must be that these individuals are rehabilitated for the long-term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, we want this process to have long-term benefits and, therefore, the approach must not only be intensive, it has to be holistic.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And by that, I mean that we would have to cover several key aspects: religious, psychological and social rehabilitation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are the three core aspects of the rehabilitative approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The approach will then have to be customised to the individual's own context.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On religious rehabilitation, there needs to be counselling sessions, but it has to be religious counselling with persons who are able to provide these self-radicalised youths proper religious teachings and interpretations that can effectively counter the radical ideology that they had somehow imbibed from online and other sources.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For that, we are fortunate in Singapore, we have the Religious Rehabilitative Group to draw our counsellors from.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, in terms of psychological rehabilitation, quite often, among these self-radicalised youths, there is propensity for hatred and violence and also a certain vulnerability to radical influence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To deal with it, the psychologists need to help them to reframe their faulty reasoning, and this effort, is actually quite an involved one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, we also need to pay attention to social rehabilitation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the self-radicalised youths are granted weekly family visits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Why that is important is because they need to preserve a connection as much as possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If they have no connection to family, you can well imagine why it will raise their risk of falling down the same path again.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Here, we also assign an after-care officer to each detainee's or supervisee's family to provide social and other support because there may be some other factors that are contributing to this person's propensity to be radicalised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Specifically, for youths, we pay additional attention to the fact that, at that stage of their lives, there is also the questions of identity and how one develops a sense of belonging.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To whom does one identify with, and with whom does one belong?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this regard, helping them to acquire critical thinking skills to discern radical rhetoric online and also to cultivate a certain mental resilience to cope with life stressors – these are the areas that we pay particular attention to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For youths, another key motivation is to complete their education and we find that, if this is a practicable thing to do, helping them to continue their studies keeps them focused, and this is something that we always try to do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I will not want to downplay the challenges.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some of the youth detainees take much longer than others to come around and this is why ISD also works with our educators to try and equip them to identify potentially self-radicalised youths early so that we can help them avoid going down this path.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And when we saw more and more restrictions, and the situation got deeper into COVID-19, YRSG made an intensified effort to engage potential employers knowing that it may be challenging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Fortunately, with their hard work, we were able to not only get the existing employers to continue to work with us, 292 new employers came on board in 2020.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we would like to sincerely thank all the supporters, employers and those who really give the fullest support to our ex-offenders and YRSG.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We are confident that with their continuous support, we will be able to help more and more ex-offenders and their families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I was very interested in the development that Minister of State Faishal stated about how to determine the danger of new psychoactive substances through the avenue of their outcome or their effect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think this will be a major advantage because, up to this stage, it has been decided via what is under the Schedule of drugs as being illicit and the weight of the drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If we are now looking at new psychoactive substances ill effects, and then calibrating punishments according to that, I think is a major development.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I am actually quite interested to learning a little bit more about how this is going to translate into the punishment regime for those who traffic in new psychoactive substances, and also in the regime for those who abuse new psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And in effect, it is a tool that I am quite excited about, because it is a new tool in the arsenal of the MDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, essentially, the exemption clause will cover substances that are already regulated under the existing regulation or those with legitimate uses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, legitimate business, commercial and scientific interest will not be affected by the NPS legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And in doing so, we have also looked at other legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we will share more details in the Second Reading for the Misuse of Drugs Bill soon.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In fact, it is a very interesting development because if I may suggest, it need not just be restricted to new psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If there is going to be a policy shift to look at the effect or the outcome of a drug on an abuser, there is no reason why to restrict it only to new psychoactive substances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That philosophy or that policy could also extend to more traditional drugs such as heroin, opium, cocaine, ketamine, ice and so on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because if we are looking at outcomes, then I think it makes a little bit easier to deter the supply you can get purer and purer forms of traditional drugs which then render the weight, the previous formula of deciding the danger of the drug, renders it outdated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, would you consider this new approach to even traditional drugs, is my question to the Minister of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If you look at the current situation as in what is happening around the world, for the more traditional drugs, it is very clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It is easy for us to determine the outcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: You get the list being updated and if you try to use different combinations, chemical structures, you realise that it is a chasing game.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we feel that while we will study all the other developments, including the traditional drugs, but one thing that we want to really catch on is how we can address the issue NPS effectively and better, in the name of protecting our people, especially our young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nevertheless, I will take on board the suggestion that the Member has made.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I very much appreciate the work of our Singapore Prison Service as Captains of Lives and I just have two follow ups.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: As some of the family situations are very complex, how can prisons better work with FSCs or enhance aftercare or introduce more family counselling and parenting skills programmes to inmates and their families?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We work with the ex-offenders to see how we can better understand and get to know more information – what is needed on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And we are going to roll this out to the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And also, in relation to the training of our volunteers, our staff who are involved in such work, we want them to better understand the landscape that they are facing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, today, we are looking at how we provide more of the very broad perspective of how they can support in terms of counselling and so forth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As we move forward, we will take on Ms Nadia's idea of how we can also provide training that will touch on the different profiles of families who may be affected by such incarceration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, I thank Ms Nadia for her suggestion and ideas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And with this, Prisons and MSF are going to work together closely with the FSCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I am confident we are able to not only reach out to more people, but we are able to have more targeted help and assistance to those who are affected by incarceration.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Murali Pillai, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, my thanks to all the hon Members of Parliament for speaking on the MHA COS debate, the four political office holders for their responses and detailing the plans and emphasis points for MHA and Home Team.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And also, most importantly, my thanks to the officers of MHA and Home Team for performing their duties 24 hours a day, every day of the year, without fear or favour, in keeping Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With that, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
